title: FASE Reading Is More Than a Reading Routine
author: SoL in the Wild
summary: The pseudonymous teacher behind SoL in the Wild argues that FASE reading is not only a fluency and accountability routine but a tool for managing cognitive load and building organized schemas as a class reads together. The starting point is that novices reading unfamiliar material must decode, hold, connect, and prioritize at once with limited working memory and few existing schemas. Using a lesson on a Ugandan microentrepreneur, the author shows how previewing the conceptual purpose of each section gives upcoming details a framework before students read them. Each chunk is followed by call and respond questions and a think, turn and talk, all hands up, cold call sequence, grounded in the principle that memory is the residue of thought. The piece concludes that the three guiding questions are not separate comprehension checks but the conceptual structure through which students organize and retain what they learned.
points: Previewing the purpose of each upcoming section turns a string of facts into chunks that fit a larger conceptual structure.
Call and respond questions double as attention checks and as a way to steer students toward the details worth remembering.
The deliberate sequence of read, think, talk, retrieve, and articulate makes students process each chunk rather than simply encounter it.
Partner talk is justified as cognitive work, not engagement, because it is tied directly to the chunk just read.
quotes: It is a multifunctional platform. I use it to hold students accountable for their attention, make reading a more social exercise, and help students improve their fluency.
Working memory is limited. When students are novices in a particular domain, they also have fewer existing schemas to help them organize and make sense of the new information.
Those statements are doing more than telling students what they are about to read. They give the upcoming information a conceptual framework.

The principle is fundamental: Memory is the residue of thought. If I want students to remember something, I need to create opportunities for them to actively think about it rather than simply encounter it in a text.
That makes the partner conversation more than an engagement strategy. It is another opportunity to think about the content.

Those are not three disconnected comprehension questions. They are the conceptual framework through which I want students to think about and organize what they learned because memory is the residue of thought.
